chunks: Why brushes wear out. The question: Why do brushes wear out?
Brushes wear out because they slide on a moving surface and also carry current through it.
Three things remove material: rubbing friction, tiny sparks, and chemistry in the air and on the surface.
These effects feed each other, which is why a motor can seem fine and then fail quickly.
Think of rubbing a pencil eraser on a table. The harder you press, and the longer you rub, the more of it you wear away.
A brush works like that eraser against the spinning commutator. Add sparks and a dry or dirty surface, and the wear gets faster.
The analogy has a gap: an eraser has no sparks, and sparks roughen the surface, which then wears the brush even faster.
With these assumed numbers the brush reaches the 6 mm wear limit at about 7400 h (0. 3 N), 4400 h (0. 5 N) and 2200 h (1. 0 N).
Life is inversely proportional to spring force and to speed. The real wear coefficient k s differs by grade and condition by orders of magnitude; the scaling is the useful part.
Friction wear: material rubbed off by sliding, roughly force times distance. Arcing: small sparks as the brush switches between segments.
Film: a thin layer on the commutator that lubricates the brush. Spring force: how hard the brush presses on the commutator. Commutator: the copper segments the brush slides on.
Friction wear is roughly proportional to contact force times sliding distance. Double the spring force and the wear doubles.
Run the motor twice as fast and the brush slides twice as far each second, so the wear rate doubles again. Both together give about 2 times 2 = 4 times the wear.
A rough commutator makes the brush bounce, which causes sparks, which make it rougher. That is the whole idea: force, distance, sparks and surface condition all add up.
"Brushes wear from three things at once. Mechanical: friction against the moving commutator removes material in proportion to spring force times sliding distance.
Electrical: commutation sparks erode the contact, and current heats the contact spots.
Chemical and environmental: graphite needs a film and humidity to lubricate, so dry air, altitude, oil or silicone make it wear fast.
A rough or out-of-round commutator makes the brush bounce, which makes sparks, which makes everything worse."
